column3: Directly parallels 75:2's oath formula, showing the particle-oath construction is not confined to self-reproach.
Its withheld exception offers only a distant contrast to an oath and does not clarify the reproaching self directly.
Pairs care for one's own self with a shared return and disclosure of deeds, joining personal responsibility to final accounting.
Directly parallels 75:2's oath formula while its object differs, keeping the oath's function open beyond a single reading.
The adjacent oath frames 75:2 with resurrection, so self-reproach stands beside rather than replaces eschatological witness.
The blamed outcome shifts culpability onto the responsible party, paralleling blame becoming manifest rather than merely alleged.
Another close formal parallel confirms that the oath formula can introduce a solemn evidentiary frame with varied objects.
Within the same passage, what one advanced and delayed is disclosed, supplying the temporal content that self-reproach may assess.
Removal of blame from the messenger contrasts with blame being located where response to warning lies.
A close oath-form parallel broadens the construction from inward selfhood to what is seen, without deciding a single function for it.
Unexpected collapse illustrates unanticipated consequence, only indirectly related to inward self-reproach.

Its life-for-life measure makes each self morally weighty; this is legal accountability rather than inward blame.
The neighboring challenge about reassembly places the self-reproach oath inside a dispute over human return.

The worship distinction supplies no clear link to self-reproach, oath, or inward witness.
The lunar collapse is part of the immediate crisis sequence that situates the oath beside overwhelming disclosure.
Prohibitions concerning wealth and selves connect harm within the community to accountable self-regard, though not specifically self-blame.
Knowledge of what is within selves is reserved to God, qualifying any reading of 75:2 as exhaustive self-knowledge.
The paired threats from below and above add a remote image of vulnerability, not a direct account of inward reproach.
Self-purification claims contrast with a self that censures rather than certifies itself; the verse also reserves just valuation to God.
Inability to help either others or themselves offers only a general negative contrast to responsible agency.
The immediate assertion of detailed re-creation makes the oath's self part of an embodied resurrection context.
No self is wronged and recompense follows deeds, giving a judicial horizon for self-assessment without equating it with inner testimony.
The inability of invoked beings to aid themselves is a distant contrast to a self capable of reproach.
No refuge in the same crisis sequence reinforces exposure, but does not itself identify the reproaching agent.
Calling attention to selves may support inward reflection, though it does not specify blame or testimony.
The departure of selves amid worldly trial makes mortal life a setting where inward accountability is tested.
The collapse of a household is an external judgment image with only a remote relation to self-reproach.
The speaker limits authority to self and brother, distinguishing personal responsibility from collective wrongdoing.
Prior blame is revisited amid coercion, showing how accusation can be socially redirected rather than inwardly owned.
In the same sequence, offered excuses stand beside the self's awareness, making self-reproach compatible with and resistant to self-defense.
Plotting returns upon the plotters' selves; this supports self-directed consequence without relying on its rejected figurative extension.
Mutual blame after a collective failure supplies a public counterpart to reproach, including both reciprocal accusation and acknowledged fault.
The startled sight belongs to the immediate disclosure scene, helping frame the self-reproach oath within perceptual shock.
Its defined sphere of being unblamed shows blame can depend on boundaries and authorization, not merely desire.
Being cast away as blameworthy links wisdom's prohibitions to accountable consequence, though it is not inward self-testimony.
The self beautifies an act after a claimed explanation, sharply pairing inward rationalization with culpable action.
A public pledge can turn back upon one's own self when broken, linking outward commitment and inward responsibility.

The same passage's final settling with the Lord supplies the destination before which self-reproach is meaningful.
A common self and intimate pairing offer a secondary account of human selfhood, not moral self-censure.
A near-identical oath formula with a distinct cosmic object confirms that 75:2 need not be reduced to one oath-object relation.
The human desire to continue ahead in transgression supplies a motive-level counterpressure to the reproaching self.
Pairing selves permits a parallel reading of relational reckoning and a secondary reading of self matched with its record.
The tranquil self supplies a deliberate counterpoint: inward life can be settled as well as reproaching, without collapsing either state.
An oath joined to settled intent and later failure shows vows, plans, and blame can move from inward resolve to exposed outcome.
What no self knows about recompense extends the limits of inward expectation, but only indirectly concerns self-reproach.
A formal oath parallel, coupled with asserted power, reinforces the solemn argumentative role of the construction.

Good advanced for selves links present action to later finding, a practical horizon for self-accounting.

Division or apportionment is only a lexical-side parallel and adds no clear account of inward blame.

The search for escape in the same passage makes self-reproach part of a crisis where evasion fails.
Its restricted state of being unblamed reinforces that blame has defined boundaries rather than being absent altogether.
Prior oaths of permanence are overturned by impending judgment, contrasting confident denial with later recognition.
Its unequal division concerns apportionment; the available auxiliary associations do not establish a link to 75:2.
Mutual accusation cannot keep concealed matter hidden, paralleling the pressure from blame toward disclosure.
Strong oaths followed by loss show that emphatic public assurance does not settle inward commitment or outcome.

The verse holds divine permission alongside the demand to reason, offering a secondary tension between enabling conditions and responsibility.
The contrast between blindness and sight supplies a limited analogue for inward discernment while retaining the prophet's epistemic limits.

The divided group is only a distant lexical parallel and adds no clear inward-accountability content.
A guardian over every self supports both continuity of the person and preservation of hidden intention, without making the guardian identical to self-reproach.
Treating one's own self foolishly presents self-directed misjudgment as a moral loss.

No earthly ransom can substitute for the wrongdoing self, making accountability nontransferable despite hidden regret.
Commanded conduct, rather than amplified oaths, is the relevant measure; this contrasts outward claims with accountable action.
God knows what is within selves, while forgiveness attends repeated return; this preserves both inward reality and divine judgment beyond self-report.
The messenger's limited responsibility gives a distant parallel to distinguishing one's own blame from another's fate.
Acknowledging wrong done to oneself and seeking forgiveness gives a reparative counterpart to self-reproach rather than an excuse for it.
Intense oaths do not guarantee belief, separating verbal assurance from the inward response it claims to predict.

No self can answer for another or secure substitute aid, giving a strong horizon of individual liability.
Those who lose themselves despite recognition show that self-loss can coexist with available knowledge, deepening the stakes of inward refusal.
A deceptive oath illustrates how sworn speech can manipulate trust and conceal intention, a contrast to truthful self-reproach.
Returning to themselves produces an admission of wrongdoing, a close narrative analogue to inward reproach even though it is quickly resisted.
Deeds rather than wishes determine recompense, restraining any reading that treats inward feeling alone as sufficient.
Testing through loss of selves and goods provides a broad trial context, not a specific account of blame.
Indecision between groups has no clear relation to the reproaching self in this evidence.
Cosmic dismantling supplies a remote eschatological backdrop without an inward-accountability link.
Striving benefits one's own self while God is independent, making moral effort self-returning rather than a benefit conferred on God.
Its lack of fear of consequence does not clearly illuminate the reproaching self.
Lying against themselves depicts self-deception as testimony against the self, closely contrasting with inward reproach.
Priority over selves introduces an ordered relation between self-interest and binding guidance, with distinct relational readings left open.
What is hidden within is brought forth publicly, linking inward concealment to disclosure rather than private control.
God's knowledge of faith and the verse's social rules provide only a secondary setting for judging inward states.
When only the accusing self is witness, repeated oaths heighten personal liability rather than replacing evidentiary responsibility.
The absence of vain or false speech is a distant contrast to excuses and self-deception.
Its protected boundaries around worship, life, and sexual conduct provide a moral field in which a self may recognize transgression.
The self's pull toward evil is the most direct counterpressure to 75:2: inward life can incite wrongdoing as well as reproach it.
The self is made sufficient as its own reckoner, closely paralleling self-witness while retaining a record-based judicial setting.
The self is given awareness of both moral ruin and guarding consciousness, directly completing the moral capacity introduced in 91:7.
The flourishing of the self through purification gives a constructive counterpart to its reproaching moral work.
The failure of the self through corruption supplies the adverse outcome against which self-reproach can operate.
Each self confronts what it advanced of good and evil, placing inward accountability in an eschatological encounter with one's acts.
Those who wrong themselves remember God and seek forgiveness, presenting self-reproach as capable of turning into repair.
Betraying one's own self frames wrongdoing as self-directed even where it harms others, reinforcing blame's inward return.
Sin acquired by a person is acquired against that person's own self, directly linking act and self-borne responsibility.
Evil attributed to one's self offers a concise counter to shifting moral fault outward, while its scope remains distinct from every kind of suffering.
A self can be delivered over to destruction by what it earns, giving an earned-consequence horizon for inward reproach.
Insight is for one's own self and blindness is against it, making moral perception personally consequential.
The warning asks whether messengers came to the selves addressed, joining warning, self-recognition, and admitted wrongdoing.
Each self earns only for itself and no bearer bears another's burden, a foundational statement of nontransferable responsibility.

Those who wronged themselves face their own admission, giving a public outcome to self-directed wrongdoing.
Wrongdoers are described as wronging their own selves, reinforcing the recurring self-harm formulation.
Wronging yourselves within sacred limits makes transgression self-directed in a communal legal setting.
Human transgression is against selves, directly contrasting apparent gain with self-directed moral loss.
Every self is tested by what it previously sent ahead, closely paralleling 75:13's disclosure of what was advanced and delayed.
Guidance benefits one's own self and misguidance is against it, distinguishing personal moral consequence from the messenger's task.
Destroyed peoples are said to have wronged themselves, framing judgment as consequence rather than arbitrary injury.
A people's condition changes when they change what is within themselves, connecting inward state to accountable transformation without reducing it to solitary blame.
Every self comes pleading for itself and is paid in full, an explicit final-accounting counterpart to the reproaching self.

Good and evil return to yourselves, giving a compact principle of self-returning moral consequence.
Guidance and misguidance attach to the guided or astray self, and no burden is borne for another.
The exposed record elicits fear over what it omits, furnishing a disclosure setting for self-reproach and excuses.
Every self is recompensed for what it strives for, directly linking individual effort to final disclosure.
No self is wronged at the scales, supplying the judicial balance within which self-reproach is neither arbitrary nor final authority.
Speech and limbs testify over what was done, providing an externalized counterpart to the self's inward witness.
God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves, repeating self-directed culpability across collective judgment.
Earlier peoples wronged themselves despite clear signs, combining available evidence with self-inflicted loss.
Disbelief is against the disbeliever, while righteous action prepares for oneself; both paths return upon the agent.
Who goes astray does so against his own self, sharply separating divine communication from personal loss.
Transgression against selves is met with an open call not to despair, making mercy a direct alternative to terminal self-condemnation.
Every self is recompensed for what it earned and none is wronged, a concise final-accounting complement.
Hearing, sight, and skins testify against their people, extending the witness motif beyond inward awareness.
The body explains its compelled testimony, complicating any reading that confines evidence to voluntary self-report.
Good is for one's self and evil is against it, paired with the assurance that the Lord does not wrong servants.
What befalls people is tied to what their hands earned, while much is pardoned; this joins consequence to mercy rather than simple equivalence.
The condemned are said to have wronged themselves, retaining the self-directed culpability formula in an afterlife setting.
Righteous work is for oneself and evil against it, followed by return to the Lord; this closely integrates agency and final return.
God knows the self's whispering, qualifying self-reproach with divine access to inward movement prior to outward speech.
God knows persons from their origination and their hidden development, so self-praise is rejected despite inward moral concern.
No burdened self bears another's burden, reinforcing the individual liability assumed by the reproaching self.
A person has only what he strives for, supplying an effort-accountability counterpart to inward self-assessment.
Forgetting God leads to forgetting one's own selves, an especially close negative image of the loss of self-reproach.
Guarding against the greed of one's self identifies an inward impulse that requires vigilance, alongside but distinct from blame.
Whoever is protected from the greed of the self succeeds, giving another direct account of inward moral danger and restraint.
Every self is held in pledge for what it earned, a compact statement of personal moral liability.
Fearing the station of judgment and restraining the self from caprice gives a practical counterpart to the reproaching self.
Every self knows what it brought forth, closely echoing 75:13-15's self-aware disclosure.
Every self knows what it sent ahead and left behind, a particularly close parallel to 75:13's temporal accounting.
No self can avail another self on that day, reinforcing the nontransferable liability surrounding 75:2.
The smallest good is seen, giving concrete scope to the self's later moral reckoning.
The smallest evil is seen, supplying the corresponding basis for even minute self-reproach.
Commanding good while forgetting yourselves presents a gap between outward moral speech and neglected self-accounting.
The community is told to turn to its Maker after wronging itself, joining grave self-directed wrong with repentance.
Treating divine signs in mockery is described as wronging yourselves, extending self-harm beyond private conduct.
What is spent for good is spent for one's own selves, another instance of moral action returning to its agent.
Every self is fully paid for what it earned at return, a direct final-accounting setting for inward reproach.
Each self earns for itself and bears the consequence of what it acquires, while the closing prayer seeks pardon and relief.
Every self is paid in full for what it earned when gathered, closely aligned with the resurrection horizon of 75:2.

Wrong done in ignorance is followed by repentance and reform, supplying a merciful path after self-directed fault.
At death, the wrongdoer's self faces exposure and humiliation, an eschatological disclosure of false claims.

Those whose scales are light are described as having lost themselves, directly joining moral measure and self-loss.

Past peoples were not wronged by God but wronged themselves, continuing the self-directed culpability pattern.

Denial despite inward certainty is described as wronging selves, a particularly close case of inward knowledge opposed by outward refusal.

Sealed mouths and testifying hands and feet provide a forceful external witness when self-exculpation is no longer possible.
Every self is paid in full for what it did, while God knows deeds completely; this joins personal recompense to comprehensive knowledge.
Receiving one's record introduces a written-accounting counterpart to the self's inward witness.
Receiving the record from behind supplies the adverse counterpart, tying one's record to exposed loss rather than private denial.
